newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Singapore says 1996 growth forecast conservative.
newsitem.headline: Singapore says 1996 growth forecast conservative.

text.p: Singapore trade and industry minister Yeo Cheow Tong said on Saturday the country's recent forecast of six percent economic growth in 1996 was "conservative".

Yeo told Reuters in an interview the country's most recent trade figures had shown the city-state's exports had picked up again after a sharp slump in the last few months, but it was too early to say if a recent economic downturn had ended.
"It would be a bit premature to conclude that we have turned round the corner just because the trade figures have picked up again. We hope we have but we really don't know," Yeo said.
Singapore announced last week a 1.1 percent year-on-year rise in its non-oil exports in October, after a 6.2 percent fall in September and a drop of 6.3 percent in August.
The Trade and Industry Ministry has blamed the export slump on the recent global slowdown in demand for electronics products.
Electronics and related products account for about half Singapore's industrial output and almost 60 percent of its non-oil exports.
The slump in exports dragged Singapore's economic growth down to just over three percent year-on-year in the third quarter from 11.4 percent in the first three months of the year.

As a result, the government said earlier this month the country's gross domestic product (GDP) would grow by about six percent this year, after an expansion of 8.8 percent in 1995 and double-digit growth in the previous two years.
But Yeo, in Manila for minister-level meetings of the 18-member Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, said he hoped Singapore's growth this year would be better than six percent.
Asked if the current six percent forecast for 1996 was conservative, Yeo said:
"Yes. We have taken a conservative approach.
"We don't know what will happen (with exports) in November and December. We hope we are wrong, but it is better to be conservative and be prepared for the worst," he said.
Yeo said Singapore industry needed to take advantage of what he called "this breather" in the pace of economic growth to develop new products and retrain its workforce.
"When the cycle picks up, new products will be needed. We have to ensure that we take this lull as a period to consolidate and be ready for the next upturn," he said.
